```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "#>", collapse = TRUE)
```

This vignette estimates population-average treatment effects for a synthetic binary outcome. For the corresponding CATE score fitting and validation, see the [binary CATE example](Binary-CATE.html). For background on binary treatment-effect prediction, see @hoogland2021binary.

## Load required packages

```{r}
library(precmed)
```

## Example data

We consider a simulated dataset of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS), in
which `relapse_count` represents the number of relapses observed during one
year of follow-up. The outcome of interest is binary: `y = 1` if a patient has
at least one relapse and `y = 0` otherwise. Relapse counts are generated using
the same model as `simulate_count()`. Everyone has the same follow-up, and the
outcome is fully observed. The `followup` argument is measured in years: `followup = 1`
means one year for every patient, while `followup = 0.5` means six months.
Set `threshold` to a larger integer to define an event as more than that many
relapses, or change `followup` to study another fixed horizon.

```{r}
binaryExample <- simulate_binary(n = 4000, seed = 2026,
                                 followup = 1, threshold = 0)
head(binaryExample)
table(binaryExample$trt, binaryExample$y)
prop.table(table(binaryExample$trt, binaryExample$y), margin = 1)
```

Treatment is assigned using age and previous treatment, so the treatment groups
need not be comparable without adjustment. Age is centered at 48 years and
previous cost is centered at 13,824 USD and divided by 20,172 USD. The
simulation coefficients are illustrative and are not clinical estimates. Unlike
a count rate ratio, the relapse risk difference depends on the selected
threshold and follow-up period.

## Estimate the average treatment effect

For the estimators and their assumptions, see [Methods for estimating average treatment effects](ATE-theory.html).

### Unadjusted treatment comparison

We first compare the observed relapse proportions under drug1 and drug0.

```{r}
relapse_risks <- with(binaryExample, tapply(y, trt, mean))
relapse_risks
```

```{r unadjusted_risk_difference, include=FALSE}
arm_sizes <- table(binaryExample$trt)
unadjusted_rd <- unname(relapse_risks["drug1"] - relapse_risks["drug0"])
unadjusted_se <- sqrt(sum(relapse_risks * (1 - relapse_risks) / arm_sizes))
unadjusted_ci <- unadjusted_rd + qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975)) * unadjusted_se
```

The unadjusted risk difference for drug1 versus drug0 is calculated by
subtracting the relapse proportion for drug0 from that for drug1. A negative
value means a lower observed relapse proportion under drug1. Here, the
unadjusted risk difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", unadjusted_rd)`, or
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * unadjusted_rd)` percentage points for drug1 minus
drug0. This unadjusted comparison may reflect
baseline differences between the groups rather than a genuine treatment effect.

The 95% confidence interval is `r sprintf("%.3f", unadjusted_ci[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", unadjusted_ci[2])`, based on a normal approximation for
two independent proportions.

### Covariate-adjusted treatment comparison

Treatment assignment may differ according to baseline characteristics. We fit
a multivariable binomial model adjusting for age, sex, previous treatment,
previous medical cost, and previous relapses, as in the count example. The
identity link estimates the risk difference directly [@naimi2020risk].

```{r}
adjusted <- glm(
  y ~ trt + age + female + previous_treatment + previous_cost +
    previous_number_relapses,
  data = binaryExample, family = binomial(link = "identity")
)
summary(adjusted)
```

```{r adjusted_risk_difference, include=FALSE}
adjusted_rd <- unname(coef(adjusted)["trtdrug1"])
adjusted_se <- summary(adjusted)$coefficients["trtdrug1", "Std. Error"]
adjusted_ci <- adjusted_rd + qnorm(c(0.025, 0.975)) * adjusted_se
```

The adjusted risk difference for drug1 versus drug0 is captured by the
coefficient for `trtdrug1` and estimated as `r sprintf("%.3f", adjusted_rd)`
(95% CI: `r sprintf("%.3f", adjusted_ci[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", adjusted_ci[2])`). The interval is a model-based Wald
interval. The model assumes that the risk difference is the same at every
covariate value; under this assumption, the coefficient is also the risk
difference averaged over the study population. A causal interpretation
requires, among other assumptions, a correctly specified outcome model, no
unmeasured confounding, and adequate treatment overlap.

### Population-level treatment comparison using `atefit()`

`atefit(response = "binary")` estimates the difference in relapse probability
under drug1 and drug0. Negative values favor drug1 because relapse is
an adverse outcome. The estimator combines a logistic outcome model and a treatment
model (the propensity-score model), which estimates the probability of receiving
treatment 1 given the covariates. Under the usual identification and regularity
assumptions, the estimator is
consistent if either model is correctly specified. Causal interpretation also
requires well-defined treatments, no unmeasured confounding, and adequate
treatment overlap. Bootstrap samples provide uncertainty estimates. These
synthetic counts do not in general imply an exactly logistic outcome model;
the treatment model is correctly specified by construction in this example.
Chapter 5, "Understanding and defining causal effects," discusses marginal
and conditional causal effects [@nguyen2026causaleffects].

The outcome formula excludes treatment: `atefit()` fits the outcome model
separately in each treatment arm. `ps.model` includes the
treatment on the left. Treatment labels are ordered as drug0 and drug1. There
is no follow-up offset for this fixed-horizon binary outcome. The default
`outcome_method = "logistic"` is currently the only available binary outcome method.

```{r}
outcome_formula <- y ~ age + female + previous_treatment + previous_cost +
  previous_number_relapses
ps_formula <- trt ~ age + previous_treatment
fit_ate <- atefit(
  response = "binary", data = binaryExample,
  outcome_model = outcome_formula, ps.model = ps_formula,
  n.boot = 100, seed = 999
)
fit_ate
```

By default, logistic regression is used for the outcome model and for the propensity model.

Use `coef()` and `confint()` to extract the risk difference and its confidence
interval:

```{r}
coef(fit_ate)
confint(fit_ate)
```

The output reports estimated population-average relapse risks of
`r sprintf("%.3f", fit_ate$risk1$estimate)` under drug1 and
`r sprintf("%.3f", fit_ate$risk0$estimate)` under drug0, shown in that
order. Their difference (drug1 minus drug0) is
`r sprintf("%.3f", fit_ate$risk.difference$estimate)`, or
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * fit_ate$risk.difference$estimate)` percentage
points. A negative difference favors drug1. The output also reports the
bootstrap standard error, a 95% Wald confidence interval of
`r sprintf("%.3f", fit_ate$risk.difference$CI.lower)` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", fit_ate$risk.difference$CI.upper)`, and a two-sided
Wald p-value for the risk difference. The causal interpretation depends on the
assumptions described above.

A causal interpretation of this estimate relies on several assumptions,
including consistency and the stable unit treatment value assumption,
conditional exchangeability, and positivity; Chapter 5 discusses these
assumptions [@nguyen2026causaleffects]. Positivity requires that both treatments
are possible at each relevant combination of covariates in the target
population. The following diagnostics summarize estimated propensity-score
overlap and treatment-weight variability in the analysis sample. They can help
investigate potential practical positivity problems, but cannot establish that
the positivity assumption holds. The table reports propensity scores before
truncation and inverse treatment weights after truncation. The outside-range
count is the number of patients whose estimated score falls outside the observed
range in the other treatment group; its percentage is within the patient's own
treatment group:

```{r overlap_atefit_call, eval=FALSE}
diagnostics(fit_ate, type = "propensity")
```

```{r overlap_atefit, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(diagnostics(fit_ate, type = "propensity"),
             digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r overlap_atefit_values, include=FALSE}
overlap <- diagnostics(fit_ate, type = "propensity", layout = "arms")
```

In this example, `r overlap$outside.other.range[1]` patients receiving drug0 and
`r overlap$outside.other.range[2]` receiving drug1 have estimated scores outside
the observed range in the other group. The effective sample sizes are
`r round(overlap$effective.n[1])` and `r round(overlap$effective.n[2])`,
respectively. The effective sample size summarizes how concentrated the
treatment weights are within each group: smaller values indicate that fewer
patients carry a larger share of the total weight, which can reduce precision.
These summaries depend on the fitted treatment model and do not
establish positivity, covariate balance, conditional exchangeability, or the
absence of unmeasured confounding. Use `layout = "arms"` for unrounded numeric
results.

Use `plot()` to inspect the bootstrap estimates:

```{r}
plot(fit_ate, metrics = c("risk0", "risk1", "risk_difference"))
```

The plot shows bootstrap relapse risks for drug0 (`risk0`) and drug1 (`risk1`),
followed by their risk difference. Red lines mark the full-sample estimates;
the dashed line marks zero in the risk-difference panel. This example uses only 100 bootstrap replicates to keep the
vignette fast; use more for an analysis. If a bootstrap model fails, the
package reports unavailable inference rather than silently dropping it.
Augmented estimates of risk are not constrained to lie within 0 and 1.

### Compare risk differences

All three estimates compare drug1 with drug0 on the same absolute probability
scale. The unadjusted comparison describes the observed treatment groups. The
identity-link binomial estimate uses the outcome model alone, whereas `atefit()`
adds a propensity-score correction. Differences between the adjusted estimates
can reflect their different models and assumptions. The unadjusted interval is
based on the two-proportion normal standard error. The binomial model uses a
model-based Wald interval; `atefit()` uses a Wald interval based on its
bootstrap standard error.

```{r compare_risk_differences, echo=FALSE}
rd_comparison <- data.frame(
  `Estimation method` = c("Unadjusted observed proportions",
                 "Adjusted binomial identity-link model",
                 "Doubly robust atefit()"),
  Interpretation = c("Unadjusted observed group difference",
                     "Conditional; also marginal under the constant-difference model",
                     "Marginal population-average difference"),
  `Risk difference` = c(unadjusted_rd, adjusted_rd,
                        fit_ate$risk.difference$estimate),
  check.names = FALSE
)
rd_comparison$`95% CI` <- sprintf(
  "%.3f to %.3f",
  c(unadjusted_ci[1], adjusted_ci[1], fit_ate$risk.difference$CI.lower),
  c(unadjusted_ci[2], adjusted_ci[2], fit_ate$risk.difference$CI.upper)
)
knitr::kable(rd_comparison, format = "html", digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             table.attr = 'class="table table-striped" style="width: auto;"')
```

The unadjusted difference compares the observed treatment groups; it is not
necessarily a causal marginal effect. The binomial model's coefficient is
conditional on the included covariates and, because it assumes the same risk
difference for every patient, equals its model-implied marginal difference.
`atefit()` targets the population-average difference without requiring a
constant conditional risk difference. Causal interpretations require the
assumptions described above.

A risk difference of -0.10 corresponds to 10 percentage points fewer patients
with a relapse under drug1. The intervals describe uncertainty around each estimate; they do
not test whether the methods differ from one another.
